title: Pricing psychology, metric framing, and discount guidance
content:
Purpose:

This is a working brief for GTM and product on how we frame pricing metrics (why tokens), structure tiers, and standardize discount language. The goal: make self-serve clear and predictable while giving sales simple levers for value-based negotiation.

High-level thesis (one line):
- Customers buy predictability + control. Pricing should signal operational efficiency (unit economics) and product simplicity (easy to understand consumption unit). Tokens do both if framed correctly.

Key framing principles (practical):
1) Single canonical metric for self-serve and developer docs
   - Use "compute tokens" as canonical consumption unit in SDK/docs. Keep conversions (characters, words, requests) as help-text only.
   - Rationale: tokens map directly to model compute and cost; they let us present tooling (estimated cost per request) without leaking hardware price complexity.

2) Tie tiers to outcome, not just throughput
   - Tier names should reflect customer outcomes: Developer, Product, Scale, Enterprise.
   - Attributes per tier: monthly included tokens, concurrency/throughput guidance, SLA/uptime, support response time, access to advanced runtime features (dedicated pools, caching).

3) Make unit economics visible (examples)
   - Show 3 example workloads (prototype, mid-PoC, production feature). For each show: expected tokens/month, recommended tier, and estimated monthly cost. This demystifies pricing and reduces demo friction.

Why token pricing (clearable bullets):
- Closest proxy to marginal compute/load on our runtime. Simple technical justification that resonates with engineering buyers.
- Enables predictable per-request forecasts (we can show average tokens per API call).
- Works across generation/embeddings/reranking without multiple unit systems.
- Avoids silly corner cases of per-request pricing (very long/very short requests) and per-conversation pricing (hidden state length).

Practical customer messaging to accompany token pricing:
- Headline: "Pay for the compute your requests use — predictable, transparent, and easy to forecast."
- Sub-line: "Tokens reflect the work the model performs. Use our estimator to see cost per call and tune prompts for better efficiency."
- FAQ points (for website/self-serve):
  * "How do tokens map to my app?" -> "We provide a token estimator in the console and SDK plus example profiles for common prompts (search, summarization, chat, embeddings)."
  * "What about embeddings vs. generation?" -> "Same tokens measure — embeddings are typically fewer tokens per call but can be more frequent; you can toggle embedding bundles in the billing UI."
  * "Do I get volume discounts?" -> brief policy summary with link to sales.

Tier structure (recommended draft):
- Developer (free / trial tier): 100k tokens included per month, community support, web console, standard models, no SLA. Good for prototyping and early evaluation.
- Product (pay-as-you-go): 5M tokens included-equivalent credit for new accounts, baseline throughput, email support, access to Optimize recommendations, token-based rate limits.
- Scale (committed / credits): commit pricing with monthly minimums, reserved capacity options (dedicated burst), 50–200ms latency-incentives, priority support, rollout controls.
- Enterprise (custom): contractual SLAs, VPC/Private deployment options, volume discounts, onboarding credits, audited logs, custom rollout and fallback policies.

Tier attributes to call out in docs and pricing page: included tokens, overage rate, concurrency guidance, supported model classes, SLA, support response time, access to Dedicated/Private, audit & compliance add-ons.

Discounting guidance (sales + self-serve):
- Default public overage pricing should be visible and rigid. Discounts should be conversation-driven, require value justification, and be documented in offers.
- Discount levers sales can use (ranked by preference):
  1) Commit term length (12–36 months) — prefer term-based discounts tied to committed monthly tokens.
  2) Upfront payment — encourages cash flow; modest additional discount for prepay beyond term discount.
  3) Product bundling — attach Optimize/Observability retention add-ons at bundled price.
  4) Usage tier gating — larger discounts only at higher volume bands (e.g., >100M tokens/month).

Do/Don't language for public-facing discount wording (short snippets):
- Do: "Volume and committed term discounts available for teams with predictable usage. Contact sales to explore options."
- Don't: "Contact sales for custom pricing" (too vague). Instead include a short value proposition: "We can help you optimize cost by recommending caching, batching, and reserved capacity — ask sales for a tailored plan."

Competitive callouts (notes for enablement):
- Competitor A: largely per-request or per-minute pricing; friction when requests have variable length. Our message: "tokens reflect actual work" — emphasize estimator and model profiles.
- Competitor B: flat subscription plus throttles — good for simple budgets but brittle at scale. Our message: "predictable economics + scale controls (commits & reserved capacity)."
- Quick battlecard bullets to prep SDRs:
  * If they complain about token math -> show token estimator + migration guide + sample cost savings using caching.
  * If they want invoice-level predictability -> pitch commit-based Scale plans with committed tokens and rollover windows.

Sales scripts (short templates):
- Self-serve lead: "Try our Developer tier with 100k free tokens — use the estimator to model your calls. When you hit predictable monthly volume, we can map you to a Scale commitment and help you save on unit costs."
- AE exploratory: "What's your monthly call pattern and typical response length? We can run a quick workload profile and recommend a tier plus 2 pragmatic levers — caching and reserved capacity — to cut unit cost by X–Y% in most cases."

Example unit-economics table (illustrative numbers, hide in internal docs):
- Small bot: 150 tokens/call, 200k calls/month -> 30M tokens -> recommend Scale or Enterprise POC.
- Search rerank: 40 tokens/query, 2M queries/month -> 80M tokens -> commit pricing band.
- Embedding pipeline: 0.5k tokens/row, 500k rows/month -> 250M tokens -> consider batch/async ingestion discounts and Dedicated pools.

Guidance for UX & Console copy (short):
- Pricing page: show "common workloads" calculator and a simple slider to pick tokens/month -> show recommended tier and estimated monthly cost.
- Billing UI: show running forecast, last 7-day token burn rate, and estimated end-of-month spend (with a toggle for conservative/aggressive prompt lengths).

Open questions / decisions to make (working list):
1) Publicly show a single example of conversion (e.g., avg tokens per minute of chat). Does this help or confuse non-technical buyers?
2) How granular should overage pricing be displayed? Flat per-token or banded?
3) Mechanic for unused committed tokens: rollover, credits, or forfeiture? (Recommend limited 3-month rollover window.)

Immediate next steps (owners):
- (Avery) Draft pricing page language and examples for dev/docs (due 2024-11-01).
- (Diego) Build 3 workload profiles with realistic token counts from infra logs (due 2024-11-15).
- (Sana + Product) Propose default overage rates and commit discount bands (due 2024-11-22).

Quick TODOs and friction notes (internal):
- Add a small "token literacy" explainer to the signup flow. Some PMs hate token math; make it optional and visual.
- Capture 5 real customer prompts in examples (help sales show prompt-efficiency wins).
- Pricing page must link to Optimize tooling for concrete ways to reduce spend (caching, quantization suggestions, batching).

Appendix: Suggested micro-copy
- "Tokens are how we measure the compute your request uses — smaller prompts, smarter prompts, and caching mean fewer tokens and lower cost."
- "Estimate cost per call in the console; switch to committed capacity when you want predictable unit pricing and priority throughput."

Open brainstorming snippets (notes to self):
- Could experiment with a "bundle" SKU for embeddings (prepaid bundles of 10M embedding tokens) — easier for data pipelines.
- Consider a loyalty credit for long-term customers who run monthly evals/runs (promotes usage of Optimize).

End of note.

Unresolved: include legal-approved language for refunds/credits, and finalize rollover policy.
